title: Faking it

fn.en: Talk about work skills; talk about obligation, permission and possibility.

gr: have to, must, don’t have to, can and be allowed to

can.en: I can say what I have to do at work, what I don’t have to do, and what I’m allowed to do.

rc: can, could, be able to and manage to

acts.say: Say which column your own job or studies fall into.

items.x: Turn up on time every morning.
Wear a suit at the weekend.
Come in on your day off.

items.r: the time by which something must be finished
do several things at the same time
plan for what is coming rather than react to it
a small group of people who judge or decide something
find time for something although you are busy

items.s: Speaking in front of a large group is one of the most ___ things you can do.
You need to be very ___ with children who are learning to read.
As a chef you have to work to ___ times — thirty seconds matters.
He took full ___ for the mistake, which surprised everybody.
She showed me one simple ___ and my whole method changed.
The driving ___ shouted “Faster!” the whole way round.

items.q: She has a real ___ for food — she talks about nothing else.
He works ___, forty hours a week, with two days off.
The team ___ him because he never asks them to do what he would not do.
Ed used to sell burgers from a ___ near the station.
I was ___ when they offered me the job on the same day.
Every Monday we ___ goals for the week ahead.

sub.en: Obligation, no obligation, permission or prohibition? Read the whole sentence first.

items.q: He ___ turn up on time — the van opened at eleven and the queue was already there.
items.why: have to = the situation or the rules make it necessary.

items.q: He ___ take much responsibility, because his boss dealt with the money.
items.why: don’t have to = it is not necessary. It does NOT mean it is forbidden.

items.q: You ___ use your phone in the kitchen. It is against the rules.
items.why: not allowed to = forbidden. Compare don’t have to = not necessary.

items.q: I ___ finish this tonight — the deadline is nine tomorrow morning.
Staff ___ take home food that would otherwise be thrown away.
In my last job we ___ wear a uniform, but most people did.
You ___ tell anybody about this. It is confidential.
items.why: mustn’t = it is forbidden. don’t have to = it is optional. They are opposites.

items.q: ___ I leave early on Friday?

rows: You have to turn up on time.
You don’t have to wear a uniform.
You can take a day off.
You aren’t allowed to use your phone.
He had to be polite to customers.

lines: In the van, Ed [had to|must|was allowed to] be reliable and turn up on time.
He [didn’t have to|mustn’t|couldn’t] get up early, because the van opened at eleven.
Now he [has to|is allowed to|doesn’t have to] manage a team, and he [must|can|doesn’t have to] work to tight deadlines.
He [isn’t allowed to|doesn’t have to|needn’t] leave until the last order is finished.
On the other hand, he [doesn’t have to|mustn’t|isn’t allowed to] work outside in February.

items.from: It is necessary for you to be here at eight.
items.cue: Rewrite it with HAVE TO. Begin: You…
items.a: You have to be here at eight

items.from: It is not necessary for you to wear a uniform.
items.cue: Rewrite it with HAVE TO. Begin: You don’t…
items.a: You don’t have to wear a uniform
alt: You do not have to wear a uniform

items.from: Using your phone in the kitchen is forbidden.
items.cue: Rewrite it with ALLOWED. Begin: You aren’t…
items.a: You aren’t allowed to use your phone in the kitchen
alt: You are not allowed to use your phone in the kitchen

items.from: Staff have permission to take home the leftover food.
items.cue: Rewrite it with CAN. Begin: Staff…
items.a: Staff can take home the leftover food

items.from: In that job it was necessary to be polite to customers.
items.cue: Rewrite it in the past with HAD TO. Begin: In that job you…
items.a: In that job you had to be polite to customers

items.from: Telling anybody about it is completely forbidden.
items.cue: Rewrite it with MUSTN’T. Begin: You…
items.a: You mustn’t tell anybody about it

items.why: mustn’t = forbidden. Something optional takes don’t have to.
must has no do form in questions: Do you have to…? or simply Must you…?
must has no past form; use had to.
RECYCLED from Lesson 7: manage + to + infinitive.

acts.title: Faking it
text: There is a television format that has run in a dozen countries. It takes somebody with no experience of a particular job, sends them to live and train with an expert for four weeks, and then puts them into a contest against professionals. A panel of judges has to decide which of the competitors is the real thing. Very often they choose wrong.

Ed was one of them. Before the programme he worked in a burger van. He had to be reliable and he had to turn up on time, and he had to be polite to customers, but he didn’t have to take much responsibility, because his boss dealt with the money. He didn’t need to get up early — the van opened at eleven — and he could take a day off more or less whenever he wanted to.

Four weeks later he was working as a chef. Now he has to manage a team, which he finds difficult, and he must work to very tight deadlines. He isn’t allowed to leave until the last order is finished. On the other hand, he doesn’t have to stand outside in February, and he can take home food that would otherwise be thrown away.

What the programme really measures is not skill. Four weeks is not long enough to learn a trade. It measures whether somebody can behave like a professional: whether they can set goals, think ahead, work under pressure and stay pleasant when a service goes wrong. The judges are not fooled by technique. They are fooled by confidence.
Which raises an uncomfortable question. If a panel of experts can’t tell the difference after four weeks, how much of any job is really the work itself?

items.s: The people on the programme have four weeks of training.
The judges usually identify the real professional correctly.
In the burger van, Ed was responsible for the money.
As a chef, Ed has to work to tight deadlines.
Ed is allowed to go home before the last order is finished.
The writer says four weeks is enough to learn a trade properly.

tts: When he was working in the burger van, Ed had to be reliable and turn up for work on time.
He also had to be polite to the customers.
However, he didn’t have to take much responsibility, as his boss dealt with the money.
He didn’t need to get up early, because the van opened at eleven.
When he wanted to, he could even take a day off work.
Now that he is training to be a chef, it is very different. He has to manage a team, and he must work to tight deadlines.
However, he doesn’t have to work outside any more, and he can take home really nice food when the restaurant has closed.

items.s: In the van, Ed had to be polite to customers.
In the van, Ed had to look after the money.

As a chef, Ed has to manage a team.
As a chef, Ed still has to work outside.

items.sit: A new colleague asks whether the uniform is compulsory. It is optional.
o: You don’t have to wear it.
You aren’t allowed to wear it.

items.sit: A new colleague asks about phones in the kitchen. They are banned.
o: You aren’t allowed to use them in there.
You don’t have to use them in there.
You needn’t use them in there.

items.sit: You are explaining the one absolutely fixed rule about the alarm.
o: You must lock up before you leave.
You must to lock up before you leave.
You have lock up before you leave.

items.sit: You are asking permission to leave an hour early on Friday.
o: Can I leave early on Friday?
Must I leave early on Friday?
Have I leave early on Friday?

items.sit: You are describing a rule from a job you had five years ago.
o: In that job I had to wear a suit.
In that job I must wear a suit.
In that job I have to wear a suit.

That’s better than my last place.

write.q: Write the rules of your job or your studies for somebody starting tomorrow. Include at least one have to, one don’t have to, one aren’t allowed to and one had to about a job you did in the past.
write.ph: On your first day you have to…
plan: how it compares with a job you had before
write.model: On your first day you have to arrive at half past eight and sign in at reception. You must read the safety sheet before you go into the workshop — that one is not negotiable. You don’t have to wear a uniform, although most people do, and you don’t have to answer emails after six. You aren’t allowed to bring visitors past the second door. In my last job I had to wear a suit every day and I wasn’t allowed to leave before my manager did, so this is a real improvement.

speak.q: Explain the rules of your job or studies out loud, as if a new person were standing in front of you. Make the difference between “you don’t have to” and “you aren’t allowed to” absolutely clear.
speak.model: So, you have to be here by half past eight, and you must read the safety sheet before you go in. You don’t have to wear a uniform — that’s up to you. But you aren’t allowed to take visitors past the second door. In my last job I had to wear a suit every day, so believe me, this is easy.
